intro: A neuron you can fire, in four tabs. Threshold: drag the excitatory input (and the inhibitory one) and watch the charge build; past threshold, sodium ions rush in and the neuron fires the same full action potential every time, which jumps down the myelinated axon. Refractory period: drag a second pulse closer to the first and see when it cannot fire the neuron. Myelin: strip stretches of myelin and time the signal. Synapse: add an agonist, an antagonist or a reuptake inhibitor and watch the receptors respond.
howItWorks:
The trace is a simple model, not a recording. The neuron rests at −70 mV and fires when its membrane reaches −55 mV (typical textbook values; real neurons vary). A brief stimulus raises the membrane and fades over a few milliseconds; if it reaches threshold, the model draws the same action potential every time: a rise to +40 mV, a fall below rest, and a return. For 2 ms after a spike nothing can fire the neuron (the absolute refractory period), and until 5 ms a stronger push is needed (the relative refractory period). A held stimulus fires the neuron again as soon as it can, so a stronger one fires more often (the practice traces use it). Inhibitory input pushes the membrane down by the same rule, so the neuron adds excitatory and inhibitory input before it decides. On the axon a myelinated stretch takes 0.12 ms and a bare one 0.9 ms: real myelin speeds a signal far more, but a bigger gap could not be watched.

The synapse is an explanatory model in relative units: one release of neurotransmitter, the share of receptors it activates, and how fast reuptake clears it. An agonist adds its own activation, an antagonist keeps most receptors from being activated, and a reuptake inhibitor slows the clearing. The neurotransmitters are the eight the course lists; the drugs are real, classed as introductory psychology classes them.

contexts.lead: In a neuroscience lab, a student records the membrane potential of one neuron in a slice of brain tissue.
A researcher stimulates a single neuron through a fine electrode and records its membrane potential.
A sensory neuron in the fingertip is pressed lightly and then firmly while its membrane potential is recorded.
A pharmacology class sorts drugs by what they do at the synapse.
A research team tests new compounds on neurons in a dish.
In a clinic, a doctor explains how a medication works.
Everyday life is full of neurotransmitters at work.
A biology teacher points to a drawing of a neuron.
